questions.topic: A chance-corrected agreement statistic
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of how well a map agrees beyond chance
questions.stem: I want to check whether two of my land cover maps of the apiary agree better than a random guess would give.

answer.exemplar: Build a confusion matrix between the two maps over the same cells, then compute the observed agreement and the agreement expected purely from the class proportions, and express the difference as a proportion of the gap between one and the chance agreement. Repeat this on several separate blocks of the apiary so the result is not driven by one lucky area.

questions.explanation: The statistic removes the part of the agreement that the class proportions alone would produce, so only the match above chance is left. Testing on several blocks checks the result holds beyond one area.
questions.hint: Compare observed agreement with chance agreement.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Kappa and accuracy pulled apart by an unbalanced sample
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a chance-corrected statistic falls when classes are unbalanced
questions.stem: Explain why the chance-corrected agreement of my land cover maps falls even though the maps agree almost everywhere.

answer.exemplar: With one dominant class the chance agreement is already high, because random pairings would often match simply by putting the common class in both maps. The chance-corrected statistic removes that large chance term, so the numerator is small while the denominator is also small, and the ratio falls even though the maps match on most cells.

questions.explanation: A dominant class pushes the chance agreement up, so the statistic must remove a large expectation of matches that never depended on the maps being good. The remaining improvement above chance can be small even when most cells agree.
questions.hint: A common class inflates the chance agreement.

answer.exemplar: Pick a sample of locations from the map that includes the classes you care about, visit each one, record the true class independently, and compare it with what the map shows at that point. questions.stem: I need to design a repeated visit survey that will let me estimate whether a hedgerow is occupied by a colony.

answer.exemplar: Select the sites from a frame that covers the whole area, visit each chosen site several times within a short season so that conditions are comparable, and record a detection or a non-detection on every visit including the ones with no sign of the colony. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Producer's and user's accuracy from the same cells
questions.learningObjective: Explain why producer's and user's accuracy can disagree
questions.stem: Explain why the producer's accuracy and the user's accuracy for the same class can be very different.

answer.exemplar: The producer's accuracy is measured from the true cells of a class while the user's accuracy is measured from the cells the map gave that class, and the two denominators differ whenever the map over- or under-labels the class. A class mapped onto too many cells then has a high producer's accuracy but a low user's accuracy, because many of the labelled cells are not that class at all.

questions.explanation: The two measures use different denominators, the true cells on one side and the mapped cells on the other, so over-labelling a class raises one and lowers the other. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions about the same class.
questions.hint: One is counted from truth, the other from the map.

questions.topic: A chance-corrected agreement statistic
questions.learningObjective: Compute the chance agreement from class proportions
questions.stem: One of my maps labels 60 percent of its cells as clover and the other labels 40 percent, so I need the agreement two maps would achieve by chance alone.
questions.explanation: Chance agreement adds the two ways a correct pairing can occur: 0.6 times 0.4 gives 0.24 and 0.4 times 0.6 gives another 0.24, totalling 0.48. Simply adding the two shares would give 1, which is impossible for agreement.
questions.hint: Multiply each map's shares and add the products.

questions.topic: An occupancy survey run in the right order
questions.learningObjective: Design a protocol that separates detection from occupancy
questions.stem: I need a survey protocol that will tell me whether an unused hive box holds a colony or merely seems empty on one visit.

answer.exemplar: Plan a fixed number of repeat visits to every box within a short season, spread across plausible times of day, and record on each visit whether a colony was seen and how long the search lasted. Repeating under different conditions separates a site where bees are genuinely absent from a site where they were present but missed, and it gives the detection history that an occupancy model requires.

questions.explanation: One empty visit cannot distinguish an absent colony from a missed one, so the protocol repeats the search under varied conditions and keeps the full detection history. Only then can detection be modelled and occupancy estimated.
questions.hint: Repeat under different conditions and log all.

questions.topic: A chance-corrected agreement statistic
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison that removes interpretation bias
questions.stem: I want to know whether my agreement figures are inflated by the same person interpreting the imagery and the reference data.

answer.exemplar: Have a second interpreter classify the same imagery and label the same reference cells independently, then compute the chance-corrected statistic for each interpreter against the reference and compare the two results with the original. questions.explanation: A second independent interpreter tests whether the agreement was inflated by a shared reading style, and comparing the two figures with the original shows how large that influence was. Without it the check cannot separate map error from interpretation habit.

questions.topic: Producer's and user's accuracy from the same cells
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of commission and omission on class accuracy
questions.stem: Explain how wrongly added and wrongly missed cells change the producer's and the user's accuracy of a class.

answer.exemplar: Every cell the map wrongly adds to a class raises the count the user's accuracy divides by without adding a correct cell, so the user's accuracy falls. Every true cell the map misses raises the count the producer's accuracy divides by without adding a correct cell, so that falls too. The two error types therefore pull their own measure down and push the other up.

questions.explanation: Added cells enlarge the denominator of the user's accuracy without adding correct ones, and missed cells enlarge the denominator of the producer's accuracy in the same way. Each error type depresses one measure while flattering the other.
questions.hint: Each error type inflates a denominator.

questions.topic: A chance-corrected agreement statistic
questions.learningObjective: Compute a chance-corrected statistic from agreement and chance
questions.stem: For my two apiary maps the overall agreement is 0.90 and the chance agreement is 0.20, so I need the chance-corrected value.
questions.explanation: The agreement above chance is 0.90 minus 0.20, which is 0.70, and the gap to perfect agreement is 1 minus 0.20, which is 0.80, so 0.70 over 0.80 gives 0.875. Reporting the raw 0.90 would credit the map with the agreement that chance alone supplies.
questions.hint: Agreement above chance, over one minus chance.
